question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error.
She always / likes to / show on / her wealth.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. show on.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "She always likes to show on her wealth" contains an error in the phrasal verb used in the segment "show on".

• Rule — Phrasal Verb: The correct phrasal verb to mean "to display something proudly, often in order to impress others" is "show off", not "show on". There is no such standard phrasal verb as "show on" in English.

• Applying the rule: the segment should read "show off" instead of "show on", giving the correct sentence: "She always likes to show off her wealth."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "she always" is grammatically correct — the subject "she" and the adverb of frequency "always" are correctly placed before the main verb.

• Option 3: "likes to" is grammatically correct — the verb "likes" agrees with the third-person singular subject "she", and is correctly followed by the infinitive "to".

• Option 4: "her wealth." is grammatically correct — the possessive adjective "her" correctly modifies the noun "wealth".

NOTE

• Commonly confused phrasal verbs with "show": "show off" (to display proudly/boastfully), "show up" (to arrive/appear), "show around" (to guide someone through a place), "show in" (to lead someone into a room).

• SSC frequently tests such wrong-preposition/particle errors in phrasal verbs (e.g., "look on" vs "look after", "give up" vs "give on").

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
If it will rain tomorrow, I will stay at home.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. will rain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "If it will rain tomorrow, I will stay at home" is a Conditional Sentence (Type 1), used to express a real or highly probable future condition.

• Rule — Conditional Sentence Type 1:
◦ If-clause (condition): Subject + Simple Present Tense
◦ Main clause (result): Subject + will/shall + V1

• The if-clause must be in the Simple Present Tense, never in the future tense, even though the condition refers to a future event. Applying the rule, the segment "will rain" is incorrect and must be replaced with the simple present form "rains".

• Corrected sentence: "If it rains tomorrow, I will stay at home."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "I will" is correct — the main clause correctly uses "will" with the base verb to express the future result.

• Option 2: "at home" is correct — it is a grammatically valid adverbial phrase of place completing the main clause.

• Option 4: "If it" is correct — "If" correctly introduces the conditional clause with the subject "it".

NOTE

• The same present-tense-in-if-clause rule applies to Type 1 conditionals with "unless", "when", "as soon as", "before", "after" and other time/condition conjunctions — none of these clauses take "will".

• Compare with Type 2 (unreal present: If + Past Simple, ... would + V1) and Type 3 (unreal past: If + Past Perfect, ... would have + V3) — SSC frequently tests confusion between these three types.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Hard had she / thrown the basketball / when it fell / on the ground.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Hard had she.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses inversion (negative adverbial inversion) with the near-negative adverb "Hardly", which requires the auxiliary verb to be placed before the subject.

• Rule — Inversion with "Hardly...when":
◦ Hardly/Scarcely + had + Subject + V3 (past participle) ... when/before + Subject + V2 (simple past)
◦ This structure is used to show that one action occurred immediately after another.

• The segment "Hard had she" wrongly uses "Hard" (an adjective/adverb meaning "with great effort") in place of "Hardly" (an adverb of degree meaning "scarcely" or "barely"). The correct segment should read "Hardly had she".

• Corrected sentence: "Hardly had she thrown the basketball when it fell on the ground."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "when it fell" is correct — "when" correctly introduces the second, immediately-following action in the simple past tense.

• Option 2: "on the ground" is correct — a valid adverbial phrase of place.

• Option 3: "thrown the basketball" is correct — "thrown" is the correct past participle (V3) of "throw", correctly used after the inverted auxiliary "had".

NOTE

• "Hard" and "Hardly" are commonly confused: "hard" means "with a lot of effort/force" (e.g., "She worked hard"), while "hardly" means "barely/scarcely" (e.g., "She hardly worked").

• Similar inversion structures frequently tested by SSC: "No sooner had... than...", "Never had... when/before...", "Scarcely had... when...".

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Ramayana is an ancient Sanskrit epic; it is believed to be written around 500 BC to 100 BC.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Ramayana is an ancient.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence refers to the Ramayana, the title of a specific, well-known literary work (an epic).

• Rule — Article "the" with titles of books/scriptures/epics: Names of specific, unique books, epics and scriptures conventionally take the definite article "the" before them, e.g., "the Ramayana", "the Mahabharata", "the Gita", "the Quran", "the Bible".

• The segment "Ramayana is an ancient" is missing the required article "the" before the proper noun "Ramayana". It should read "The Ramayana is an ancient".

• Corrected sentence: "The Ramayana is an ancient Sanskrit epic; it is believed to be written around 500 BC to 100 BC."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Sanskrit epic; it is" is correct — no article or agreement error is present.

• Option 3: "believed to be written" is correct — the passive construction "is believed to be written" is grammatically valid to express a commonly held belief about the past.

• Option 4: "around 500 BC to 100 BC." is correct — a valid adverbial phrase of time.

NOTE

• The definite article "the" is also required before names of rivers (the Ganga), mountain ranges (the Himalayas), oceans/seas (the Indian Ocean), and newspapers (the Times of India), but NOT before names of single mountain peaks, lakes, or most countries.

• Commonly tested with other epics/scriptures: the Vedas, the Upanishads, the Puranas, the Iliad, the Odyssey.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The period from 1858-1905 was the seed time of Indian nationalism; and the early nationalists (1) _________ the seeds well and deep. Instead of basing their nationalism or appeals to (2) ____________ sentiments and passing emotions, or abstract rights of freedom and liberty, or on obscurantist appeals to the past, they_______(3) it in a hard-headed and penetrating analysis of the complex mechanism of modern imperialism and the chief contradiction between the interests of the Indian people and British rule. The result was that they (4) ____________ a common political and economic programme which (5) ____________ rather than divided the different sections of the people. Later on, the Indian people could gather around this programme and wage powerful struggles.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. sowed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage uses an extended metaphor of "seed time" — nationalism is compared to a field being sown with seeds. The verb needed must continue this metaphor.

• "Sowed" (past tense of "sow", meaning to plant seeds in the ground) fits perfectly with "the seeds well and deep", continuing the agricultural imagery introduced by "seed time".

• Reading the completed sentence: "...the early nationalists sowed the seeds well and deep." This flows logically into the rest of the passage, which explains how that sown nationalism later grew into a shared political programme.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "buried" is incorrect — to bury seeds means to hide/cover them permanently, which contradicts the idea of nationalism later growing and spreading.

• Option 2: "scattered" is incorrect — it suggests careless, random spreading, which contradicts "well and deep", implying a careful, deliberate act.

• Option 3: "threw" is incorrect — it does not fit the specific agricultural collocation with "seeds"; the natural, idiomatic verb for planting seeds is "sow", not "throw".

NOTE

• Common agricultural collocations tested by SSC: sow seeds, reap a harvest, plough a field, till the land, cultivate a crop.

• The idiom "to sow the seeds of something" (e.g., "to sow the seeds of discord") means to create the conditions that will later cause something to develop.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The period from 1858-1905 was the seed time of Indian nationalism; and the early nationalists (1) _________ the seeds well and deep. Instead of basing their nationalism or appeals to (2) ____________ sentiments and passing emotions, or abstract rights of freedom and liberty, or on obscurantist appeals to the past, they_______(3) it in a hard-headed and penetrating analysis of the complex mechanism of modern imperialism and the chief contradiction between the interests of the Indian people and British rule. The result was that they (4) ____________ a common political and economic programme which (5) ____________ rather than divided the different sections of the people. Later on, the Indian people could gather around this programme and wage powerful struggles.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. shallow.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence sets up a contrast using "Instead of": the nationalists did NOT base their movement on blank(2) sentiments; instead, they rooted it in a "hard-headed and penetrating analysis".

• The required word must be the opposite in spirit of "hard-headed and penetrating" (i.e., something superficial or lacking depth), since the sentence sets up a rejected alternative before describing what the nationalists actually did.

• "Shallow" (lacking depth, superficial) correctly contrasts with the later phrase "hard-headed and penetrating analysis", and also logically pairs with "passing emotions" later in the same sentence — both describe something fleeting and superficial.

• Reading the completed sentence: "Instead of basing their nationalism...on shallow sentiments and passing emotions...they rooted it in a hard-headed and penetrating analysis."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "grounded" is incorrect — "grounded sentiments" would suggest something well-founded and stable, which contradicts the passage's point that this basis was being rejected as inadequate.

• Option 3: "profound" is incorrect — it means deep/serious, the opposite of the superficial quality the sentence is describing, and would make no sense being contrasted with a "hard-headed and penetrating analysis".

• Option 4: "deep" is incorrect for the same reason as "profound" — it contradicts the intended meaning of something superficial being rejected in favour of a deeper analysis.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always look for contrast markers ("instead of", "but", "however", "rather than") — the words on either side of such markers are usually opposite in meaning or tone.

• Synonyms of "shallow" (in this sense): superficial, cursory, skin-deep.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The period from 1858-1905 was the seed time of Indian nationalism; and the early nationalists (1) _________ the seeds well and deep. Instead of basing their nationalism or appeals to (2) ____________ sentiments and passing emotions, or abstract rights of freedom and liberty, or on obscurantist appeals to the past, they_______(3) it in a hard-headed and penetrating analysis of the complex mechanism of modern imperialism and the chief contradiction between the interests of the Indian people and British rule. The result was that they (4) ____________ a common political and economic programme which (5) ____________ rather than divided the different sections of the people. Later on, the Indian people could gather around this programme and wage powerful struggles.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. rooted.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence continues the contrast begun with "Instead of": instead of basing nationalism on shallow sentiments, the nationalists blank(3) it in a hard-headed and penetrating analysis.

• "Rooted" (past tense of "root", meaning to firmly establish or base something on a solid foundation) is the natural collocation with "in" — the phrase "rooted in" means firmly based on or grounded in something.

• Reading the completed sentence: "...they rooted it in a hard-headed and penetrating analysis of the complex mechanism of modern imperialism..." — this correctly conveys that the nationalists based their movement solidly on rigorous analysis.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "controlled" is incorrect — "controlled it in an analysis" is not a meaningful or idiomatic collocation.

• Option 3: "drove" is incorrect — "drove it in an analysis" does not make idiomatic sense with the preposition "in".

• Option 4: "minded" is incorrect — "minded it in an analysis" is not a standard or meaningful collocation.

NOTE

• "Rooted in" is a common fixed collocation meaning firmly based on something, e.g., "Her confidence is rooted in years of practice."

• Other similar collocations with "in": grounded in, based in, steeped in, embedded in.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The period from 1858-1905 was the seed time of Indian nationalism; and the early nationalists (1) _________ the seeds well and deep. Instead of basing their nationalism or appeals to (2) ____________ sentiments and passing emotions, or abstract rights of freedom and liberty, or on obscurantist appeals to the past, they_______(3) it in a hard-headed and penetrating analysis of the complex mechanism of modern imperialism and the chief contradiction between the interests of the Indian people and British rule. The result was that they (4) ____________ a common political and economic programme which (5) ____________ rather than divided the different sections of the people. Later on, the Indian people could gather around this programme and wage powerful struggles.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. evolved.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes the outcome ("The result was that...") of the nationalists' careful, analytical approach described earlier in the passage.

• "Evolved" (past tense of "evolve", meaning to develop gradually, especially from a simple to a more complex form) correctly conveys that a common political and economic programme was gradually developed as a result of their analysis.

• Reading the completed sentence: "The result was that they evolved a common political and economic programme which united rather than divided the different sections of the people." This logically follows from the earlier idea of a hard-headed, penetrating analysis leading to a developed programme.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "banished" is incorrect — it means to expel or send away, which makes no sense with "a common political and economic programme" as its object.

• Option 3: "uprooted" is incorrect — it means to remove something forcibly from its place, the opposite of developing and establishing a new programme.

• Option 4: "collapsed" is incorrect — it means to fall apart or fail suddenly, which contradicts the positive, constructive result the passage describes.

NOTE

• "Evolve" is commonly used in the context of gradual development of ideas, policies, systems and living organisms.

• Distinguish from "revolve" (to move in a circle) — a commonly confused word pair in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The period from 1858-1905 was the seed time of Indian nationalism; and the early nationalists (1) _________ the seeds well and deep. Instead of basing their nationalism or appeals to (2) ____________ sentiments and passing emotions, or abstract rights of freedom and liberty, or on obscurantist appeals to the past, they_______(3) it in a hard-headed and penetrating analysis of the complex mechanism of modern imperialism and the chief contradiction between the interests of the Indian people and British rule. The result was that they (4) ____________ a common political and economic programme which (5) ____________ rather than divided the different sections of the people. Later on, the Indian people could gather around this programme and wage powerful struggles.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. united.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence contains the contrast marker "rather than", directly opposing the required word with "divided".

• Rule — "rather than" indicates contrast/antonymy: The word before "rather than" is typically the opposite in meaning of the word after it, since the sentence is stating what the programme did (not what it did NOT do).

• "United" is the direct antonym of "divided", and correctly conveys that the common political and economic programme brought the different sections of the people together instead of separating them.

• Reading the completed sentence: "...a common political and economic programme which united rather than divided the different sections of the people."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "dissolved" is incorrect — it means to break up or disintegrate, which is not the logical opposite of "divided" required here, and does not fit "different sections of the people" as its object meaningfully in this context.

• Option 3: "classified" is incorrect — it means to categorize or sort into groups, which is closer in meaning to "divided" than opposite to it.

• Option 4: "complicated" is incorrect — it means to make something more difficult or confusing, which does not form a logical contrast with "divided".

NOTE

• Look for antonym pairs signalled by connectors like "rather than", "instead of", "but not", "as opposed to" — the cloze answer is often a direct opposite of a nearby word.

• "United" and "divided" is a classic antonym pair frequently tested in SSC vocabulary and cloze questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
It took 4 hours straight to ____________ the deal with the regional company.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. close.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes finalising a business agreement over a long, continuous period ("4 hours straight").

• Fixed collocation — "close a deal": In business English, the standard, idiomatic expression for finalising or concluding a business agreement is "to close a deal".

• Reading the completed sentence: "It took 4 hours straight to close the deal with the regional company." This correctly and idiomatically conveys that the negotiation was successfully concluded after four continuous hours.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "stop" is incorrect — "stop the deal" would mean to prevent or halt the deal, which contradicts the sense of a deal being successfully completed after long effort.

• Option 2: "get" is incorrect — "get the deal" is vague and not the standard collocation used for concluding a negotiation.

• Option 3: "perform" is incorrect — "perform a deal" is not idiomatic English; "perform" collocates with tasks, duties or actions, not with "deal".

NOTE

• Other common business collocations with "deal": strike a deal, seal a deal, cut a deal, broker a deal, clinch a deal — all mean to successfully negotiate and finalise an agreement.

• Contrast with "break a deal" (to fail to honour an agreement) and "call off a deal" (to cancel an agreement).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
As I have no time to discuss the points, so I wrote a email to her.
option_1: so I wrote an e-mail for her
option_2: so I wrote a e-mail to her
option_3: I write an email to her
option_4: I wrote an email to her
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I wrote an email to her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original sentence "As I have no time to discuss the points, so I wrote a email to her" contains two errors: (i) the redundant use of "so" after "As", and (ii) the incorrect article "a" before the vowel-sound word "email".

• Rule 1 — Redundant conjunctions: When a subordinate clause begins with "As", "Since", or "Because" (all meaning "for the reason that"), the main clause must NOT begin with "so"; only one of the two conjunctions is needed to link the cause and result.

• Rule 2 — Article "a" vs "an": The article "an" is used before words beginning with a vowel sound. "Email" begins with the vowel sound /ɪ/, so it must take "an", not "a".

• Applying both rules: "so" is dropped and "a email" is corrected to "an email", giving: "As I have no time to discuss the points, I wrote an email to her."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "so I wrote an e-mail for her" is incorrect — it retains the redundant "so", and also wrongly changes the preposition "to" to "for".

• Option 2: "so I wrote a e-mail to her" is incorrect — it retains the redundant "so" and still uses the wrong article "a" instead of "an".

• Option 3: "I write an email to her" is incorrect — it wrongly changes the verb tense to the simple present "write", whereas the rest of the sentence (and the context of narrating a completed action) requires the simple past "wrote".

NOTE

• Other redundant conjunction pairs commonly tested by SSC: "Although...but", "Because...so", "Though...yet" — only one connector of each such pair should be used at a time.

• Both "email" and "e-mail" are acceptable spellings, but the article must always follow the pronunciation rule (vowel sound → "an").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
At one's fingertips
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To have complete knowledge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "At one's fingertips" means to have thorough, ready and complete knowledge of something, available for instant use. (पूर्ण जानकारी होना)
◦ Example: As an experienced doctor, he has all the symptoms of common diseases at his fingertips.

• The image behind the idiom is of something being so close and familiar — like one's own fingertips — that it can be accessed instantly without effort.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To be unaware of something (किसी बात से अनजान होना): To have no knowledge or awareness of something — this is nearly the opposite of the given idiom.

• Option 2: To take revenge (बदला लेना): To harm someone in return for a wrong done by them; unrelated to knowledge.

• Option 3: Out of reach (पहुंच से बाहर): Not accessible or attainable — again nearly opposite in sense to "at one's fingertips".

NOTE

• Other idioms about knowledge/expertise often asked in SSC: "To know something like the back of one's hand" (to know very well), "To have a good grasp of something", and "To be well versed in" (to be skilled/knowledgeable in).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Resistance
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Tolerance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Resistance" means the act of opposing, refusing to accept, or fighting against something. (प्रतिरोध/विरोध)

• Its antonym, "Tolerance", means the willingness or ability to accept, allow or put up with something, especially something one may not agree with. (सहनशीलता/स्वीकृति)

• While "resistance" involves actively opposing or refusing something, "tolerance" involves accepting and allowing it — making the two words direct opposites in the context of one's attitude towards something.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Awareness (जागरूकता): Knowledge or consciousness of something; not an opposite of resistance.

• Option 3: Tenderness (कोमलता): Gentleness or sensitivity in feeling; unrelated in meaning to resistance.

• Option 4: Reliance (निर्भरता): Dependence on someone or something; not an antonym of resistance.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "resistance": opposition, defiance, obstruction.

• Other antonym pairs related to acceptance/opposition often tested by SSC: defiance × compliance, resistance × submission, rebellion × obedience.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the bracketed word segment in the following sentence.
Children should avoid giving out personal details online (which will) identify them or their location.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. that could.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed segment "(which will)" introduces a relative clause describing the possibility, not the certainty, that certain personal details might identify a child or their location.

• Rule — Modal of possibility vs certainty: "Will" expresses certainty or a definite future outcome, whereas "could" expresses possibility — that something might happen, not that it definitely will. Since not all personal details definitely identify a person or location, only some of them possibly do, "could" is the logically correct modal here.

• The relative pronoun "that" is also more natural than "which" in this restrictive (defining) relative clause, though both are grammatically acceptable; "that could" is the standard, most appropriate substitution tested here.

• Corrected sentence: "Children should avoid giving out personal details online that could identify them or their location."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "what will" is incorrect — "what" is not used as a relative pronoun referring back to "personal details"; it functions differently (as a free relative pronoun meaning "the thing that").

• Option 3: "whichever can" is incorrect — "whichever" means "no matter which one", which does not fit the sense of a defining relative clause describing personal details in general.

• Option 4: "which might lead" is incorrect — "lead" requires a following preposition (e.g., "lead to identifying") to make grammatical sense; as written, "which might lead identify them" is not a complete, correct construction.

NOTE

• Modal verbs of possibility in increasing order of certainty: might < could < may < can < will.

• "That" is generally preferred over "which" in restrictive/defining relative clauses in formal written English, though both are commonly accepted.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The rocky terrain made the hike difficult and strenuous.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Easy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Strenuous" means requiring or showing great effort or exertion; physically demanding. (कठिन/श्रमसाध्य)

• Its antonym, "Easy", means requiring little effort; not difficult. (आसान)

• In the given sentence, the rocky terrain made the hike "difficult and strenuous" — the opposite quality of a hike would be one that is "easy", requiring little effort.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Demanding (चुनौतीपूर्ण): Requiring a lot of effort or skill; a synonym of "strenuous", not its antonym.

• Option 2: Lively (जीवंत/स्फूर्तिवान): Full of energy and enthusiasm; describes manner or mood, not physical ease, and is not the antonym of "strenuous".

• Option 3: Intense (तीव्र): Existing or occurring in a high or extreme degree; close in sense to "strenuous" rather than opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "strenuous": arduous, laborious, exhausting, taxing.

• Other antonym pairs of effort/difficulty often tested by SSC: arduous × effortless, laborious × simple, taxing × relaxing.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The road which connecting the two states is overcrowded.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. connects.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The road which connecting the two states is overcrowded" contains a relative clause — "which connecting the two states" — that lacks a finite main verb.

• Rule — Relative clauses need a finite verb: In a relative clause introduced by "which" (acting as the subject of the clause, referring back to "the road"), the verb must be a finite verb that agrees with the subject, not a bare present participle (-ing form) used without an auxiliary.

• Since "the road" (and hence "which") is singular and the general fact is stated in the present tense, the correct finite verb form is "connects" (third-person singular, simple present).

• Corrected sentence: "The road which connects the two states is overcrowded."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "connected" is incorrect — the simple past tense does not fit the general, ongoing present-tense fact being described (the road is currently overcrowded, and currently connects the two states).

• Option 3: "has connecting" is incorrect — "has" requires a past participle ("has connected") to form the present perfect, not a present participle; "has connecting" is not a valid verb form.

• Option 4: "have connected" is incorrect — besides being the wrong auxiliary for a singular subject ("the road" requires "has", not "have"), the present perfect tense does not fit the intended simple, general-fact meaning of the sentence.

NOTE

• A bare -ing form (present participle) can never function as the main finite verb of a clause on its own — it always needs an auxiliary (is/was/has been connecting, etc.) or must be replaced with a finite verb form.

• Subject-verb agreement with relative pronouns (who/which/that) follows the number of the noun they refer back to (the antecedent) — here, "the road" (singular) requires a singular verb form.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Ria is liked by everyone as she is very amicable.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Unfriendly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Amicable" means friendly, sociable, and pleasant in manner; showing goodwill. (मिलनसार/मित्रतापूर्ण)

• Its antonym, "Unfriendly", means not showing warmth or kindness towards others; hostile or cold in manner. (अमित्रतापूर्ण)

• The sentence states Ria "is liked by everyone as she is very amicable" — the opposite quality would make a person disliked, i.e., being "unfriendly".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Hateful (घृणित): Feeling or showing intense dislike; too strong and different in nuance from a plain antonym of "friendly".

• Option 3: Stupid (मूर्ख): Lacking intelligence or good judgement; describes intellect, not friendliness, and is unrelated to "amicable".

• Option 4: Dangerous (खतरनाक): Likely to cause harm; describes risk, not sociability, and is not the antonym of "amicable".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "amicable": cordial, congenial, affable, genial.

• Related antonym pairs often tested by SSC: cordial × hostile, affable × surly, genial × unsociable.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Hospital for people with mental illnesses
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Asylum.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Asylum" means an institution or hospital that provides care and shelter for people suffering from mental illness. (मानसिक रोगियों का आश्रय-स्थल/पागलखाना)
◦ Example: After the accident, he was admitted to an asylum for psychiatric treatment.

• This is a classic one-word substitution frequently asked by SSC for institutions/places related to specific groups of people.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Hangar (विमानशाला): A large building used for housing and repairing aircraft; unrelated to hospitals or mental illness.

• Option 2: Druggist (औषध विक्रेता): A person who sells medicines, i.e., a pharmacist/chemist; refers to a person, not an institution.

• Option 4: Shelter (आश्रय): A general place providing protection or refuge (e.g., from weather or homelessness); too broad and not specific to mental illness.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes often tested by SSC: Orphanage (home for orphans), Sanatorium (hospital for the chronically ill, especially for rest-cure treatment), Hospice (a home providing care for the terminally ill), Infirmary (a place for the care of the sick).

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
A distinguished academecian, Amartya Sen has taught in India, Britain and the United States.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Academecian.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "Academician" — a person who is a member of an academy, or a person associated with an institution of higher learning, especially one engaged in scholarly research and teaching.
◦ Example: As a respected academician, he has published extensively on economic policy.

• Spelling key: ACADEM + ICIAN. Note the ending "-ician" (as in "physician", "musician", "technician"), not "-ecian". The word given in the sentence, "academecian", wrongly replaces the "ici" with "ec".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Taught" is correctly spelt — the past tense/past participle of "teach".

• Option 3: "Britain" is correctly spelt — the name of the country.

• Option 4: "Distinguished" is correctly spelt — meaning notable or eminent.

NOTE

• Words ending in "-ician" denoting a person's profession/role: physician, musician, technician, politician, mathematician, magician — SSC frequently tests confusion of this ending with "-esian" or "-ecian".

• Do not confuse "academician" (a scholar/member of an academy) with "academic" (relating to education, or a person who teaches/does research at a university).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
Teja followed his friend's advice so now he is in deep water.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. In trouble.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "In deep water" means to be in a difficult, risky or troublesome situation. (मुसीबत में)
◦ Example: After missing the deadline three times, he found himself in deep water with his manager.

• The idiom draws on the image of a person swimming who has gone into water too deep to stand in, and is therefore in danger — used figuratively for any serious trouble or difficulty.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: In deep thoughts (गहरे विचार में): Absorbed in serious thinking; unrelated to trouble or danger.

• Option 2: In dilemma (दुविधा में): Facing a difficult choice between two options; close but not the precise meaning — "in deep water" denotes trouble/danger generally, not specifically a choice between two options.

• Option 4: In good position (अच्छी स्थिति में): In a favourable or advantageous situation — this is nearly the opposite of "in deep water".

NOTE

• Other idioms of trouble/difficulty often asked in SSC: "To be in hot water" (to be in trouble), "To be on thin ice" (to be in a risky situation), "To be between the devil and the deep sea" (to face two equally bad choices).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The committee deposed him from his office.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Promoted.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Deposed" means removed suddenly and forcefully from a position of power or office. (पदच्युत करना)

• Its antonym, "Promoted", means raised to a higher position, rank or office. (पदोन्नत करना)

• While "deposed" involves forcibly taking someone out of office/power, "promoted" involves elevating someone to a higher position — making the two words opposite in the context of a person's standing in an office or organisation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Interacted (बातचीत की): Communicated or engaged with someone; unrelated in meaning to removal from office.

• Option 2: Demolished (ध्वस्त करना): To pull down or destroy a physical structure; used for buildings, not usually for a person's office/position.

• Option 4: Segregated (अलग करना): To separate or set apart, typically by race, sex, or class; unrelated to removal from a position of power.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "deposed": dethroned, ousted, overthrown, unseated.

• Related antonym pairs often tested by SSC: dethrone × crown, oust × install, overthrow × instate.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Language interacts with all aspects of human life and society.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. disconnects.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Interacts" means communicates with or has an effect on; acts reciprocally with something else. (परस्पर क्रिया करना/जुड़ना)

• Its antonym, "disconnects", means breaks the connection with; separates from. (संपर्क तोड़ना/अलग होना)

• The sentence states that "Language interacts with all aspects of human life and society", meaning it is deeply connected to and influences them; the opposite would be language having no connection with, or being separated from, those aspects — i.e., it "disconnects" from them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: co-operates (सहयोग करता है): To work jointly with others towards a common goal; a near-synonym of "interacts", not its antonym.

• Option 2: interrelates (परस्पर संबंधित होता है): To be connected with or related to something else; again close in meaning to "interacts", not opposite.

• Option 4: intermingles (घुल-मिल जाता है): To mix or blend together with something; also close in meaning to "interacts" rather than its opposite.

NOTE

• Prefixes are a useful clue in antonym questions: "dis-" (as in "disconnect", "disengage", "dissociate") commonly reverses the meaning of a root word denoting connection or association.

• Other antonym pairs of connection often tested by SSC: associate × dissociate, engage × disengage, unite × separate.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Aquire.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "Acquire" — to gain or come to possess something, especially through one's own effort, skill or actions.
◦ Example: She worked hard to acquire fluency in three languages.

• Spelling key: AC + QUIRE. The word is often misspelt by dropping the "c", giving the incorrect form "Aquire" as seen in this option.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Category" is correctly spelt — a class or division of people or things.

• Option 2: "Hygiene" is correctly spelt — conditions or practices conducive to maintaining health and cleanliness.

• Option 3: "Congratulate" is correctly spelt — to express praise for an achievement.

NOTE

• Related words with the same silent-"c" + "qu" pattern often confused in spelling: acquaint, acquit, acquiesce, acquisition — all retain the "c" before "qu".

• Do not confuse "acquire" (to gain/obtain) with "inquire" (to ask) or "require" (to need) — all share the "-quire" ending but have different prefixes and meanings.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Beautiful
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Ugly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Beautiful" means pleasing to look at; possessing qualities that give great pleasure to the senses or the mind. (सुंदर)

• Its direct antonym, "Ugly", means unpleasant or unattractive to look at. (कुरूप/बदसूरत)

• Among the given options, "Ugly" is the only word that directly describes an unattractive physical appearance, making it the exact opposite of "beautiful".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Pungent (तीखा/तीव्र गंध वाला): Having a sharp, strong smell or taste; describes odour/flavour, not appearance.

• Option 2: Stingy (कंजूस): Unwilling to spend or give; describes a person's attitude towards money, not appearance.

• Option 3: Slimy (चिपचिपा): Covered with a sticky, unpleasant substance, or (figuratively) excessively flattering/untrustworthy; not the standard antonym of "beautiful".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "beautiful": gorgeous, stunning, exquisite, lovely, attractive.

• Other antonym pairs of appearance often tested by SSC: attractive × repulsive, elegant × shabby, handsome × unsightly.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word 'Defeat' in the given sentence.
The first battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526, where Babur introduced canon warfare and was able to gain victory on Delhi and subjugated sultanate ruler Ibrahim Lodi.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. victory.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Defeat" means to overcome or beat someone in a battle, contest or competition; a failure to win. (हार/पराजय)

• Its antonym, "Victory", means an act of winning or success in a battle, contest or struggle. (जीत/विजय)

• Among the four words drawn from the given sentence — gain, subjugated, warfare, victory — only "victory" is the direct semantic opposite of "defeat"; the sentence itself confirms this usage, stating that Babur "was able to gain victory on Delhi", i.e., he won rather than lost.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: gain (प्राप्त करना): To obtain or acquire something; a general verb of acquisition, not an antonym of "defeat".

• Option 2: subjugated (अधीन करना): Brought under domination or control; related in theme to conquest but not itself the antonym of "defeat".

• Option 3: warfare (युद्ध): The activity of fighting a war; a neutral noun describing conflict itself, not an antonym of "defeat".

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs related to conflict/outcome often tested by SSC: triumph × failure, conquest × surrender, success × defeat.

• Such questions test whether a candidate can locate the correct target word within a sentence before applying antonym knowledge — always re-read the sentence carefully to identify which word is actually being tested.
